channel.title: PsyDigest — psychiatry literature digest
channel.description: Summaries of new psychiatric research and guidelines

item.title: [24] Efficacy of community interventions for posttraumatic stress disorder symptoms: a Bayesian network meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study used a Bayesian network meta-analysis (NMA) of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) to compare the effectiveness of community-based interventions for posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) symptoms in trauma-exposed community populations. The clinical question was whether community-tailored or evidence-based psychotherapies are more effective in reducing PTSD symptoms in real-world settings.
FINDINGS: Thirty-six RCTs (n=5,350) compared 16 intervention types. Prolonged exposure (PE) and cognitive processing therapy (CPT) showed the strongest immediate effects on PTSD symptoms (PE: SMD = 1.69, 95% CrI [1.14, 2.24]; CPT: SMD = 1.23, 95% CrI [0.81, 1.67]). Community-tailored interventions combined showed a moderate effect (SMD = 0.52, 95% CrI [0.34, 0.71]), with individual community-tailored approaches (e.g., psychoeducation, care management, CETA) ranging from SMD 0.48 to 0.59. Secondary outcomes included reductions in depression and anxiety, and treatment attrition was reported.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence suggests trauma-focused therapies (PE, CPT) have larger immediate effects on PTSD symptoms in community settings compared to community-tailored interventions, though the latter still show moderate benefits. The NMA used robust methods (Bayesian random-effects model, Cochrane risk of bias assessment), but heterogeneity across studies and populations may limit certainty. The CrIs are wide for PE and CPT, indicating imprecision. The clinical significance of moderate effects in community-tailored interventions is plausible, especially in low-resource settings, but long-term durability beyond 6 months remains uncertain.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: PE and CPT remain first-line options for PTSD in community settings where feasible, but community-tailored interventions may offer accessible alternatives when specialist care is unavailable. Clinicians should consider patient preferences, resource availability, and trauma type when selecting interventions, while monitoring for symptom reduction and attrition.

item.title: [20] Efficacy of estrogen therapy for postpartum depression: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: Postpartum depression (PPD) is common and disabling, and a sharp drop in estrogen after childbirth has led to trials of estrogen replacement. This PRISMA-guided systematic review and meta-analysis synthesised all randomised controlled trials (RCTs) that tested estrogen versus placebo for women with PPD.
FINDINGS: Four small RCTs (n = 154) yielded a pooled standardised mean difference of −0.16 (95 % CI −0.58 to 0.25; I² = 35 %), indicating no statistically significant benefit of estrogen. The GRADE certainty of evidence was rated low because of very serious imprecision (wide CI, small sample).
INTERPRETATION: The pooled estimate is consistent with no effect, a modest benefit, or possible harm; the evidence is too weak to draw firm conclusions. The low GRADE rating reflects risk of bias in the small trials and imprecision rather than direct evidence of harm. Larger, rigorously conducted RCTs with pharmacokinetic monitoring are needed before estrogen can be considered effective or safe for routine use.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Estrogen cannot be recommended for routine treatment of PPD on current evidence; watch for emerging trial data but do not change practice yet.

item.title: [17] Non-pharmacological augmentation of trauma-focused psychotherapy for PTSD: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study asks whether adding non-pharmacological interventions to trauma-focused psychotherapy (TFP) improves outcomes in PTSD. It systematically reviews and meta-analyses 50 RCTs (39 included in meta-analysis, N = 2,853) comparing TFP + augmentation vs TFP alone or active control, classifying augmentation strategies into a three-level framework.
FINDINGS: The meta-analysis found no significant overall effects of augmentation on PTSD symptom severity (g = -0.10, p = .062), response rate (RR = 1.04, p = .111), or dropout (RR = 0.94, p = .489). A subgroup targeting sleep disturbance showed a small but significant benefit (symptom reduction g = -0.24, p = .03).
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is large and well-defined, but the overall lack of significant benefit across primary outcomes suggests that non-pharmacological augmentation does not reliably enhance TFP efficacy. The sleep-focused subgroup finding is preliminary and should be interpreted cautiously due to potential confounding and limited power. The three-level framework is a useful conceptual tool, but heterogeneity in interventions and populations limits generalisability.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence does not support routinely adding non-pharmacological interventions to TFP for PTSD outside of targeted sleep-focused strategies. Clinicians should prioritise standard TFP and consider sleep-specific augmentation only when sleep disturbance is a prominent residual symptom.

item.title: [17] Factors associated with mood and anxiety disorders in patients with cancer: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review and meta-analysis (50 cohort/case-control studies, n≥5 per factor) examined risk factors for mood/anxiety disorders or clinically significant symptoms in adult cancer survivors (breast, lung, colorectal, prostate, stomach, liver, pancreatic). The clinical question is whether identifiable factors can guide targeted screening in oncology.
FINDINGS: Pooled relative risks showed higher tumor stage (RR 1.55, 95% CI 1.21–1.97; 28 studies), more physical comorbidities (RR 1.57, 95% CI 1.34–1.84; 36 studies), prior psychiatric history (RR 4.85, 95% CI 2.77–8.50; 13 studies), female sex (RR 1.52, 95% CI 1.32–1.75; 19 studies), underweight BMI (RR 1.93, 95% CI 1.55–2.44; 6 studies), unmarried status (RR 1.35, 95% CI 1.14–1.58; 25 studies), and current smoking (RR 1.27, 95% CI 1.12–1.46; 12 studies) were associated with increased risk.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is large and mostly observational, so causality cannot be inferred. Strengths include broad literature coverage and consistent direction of effect across many studies. However, heterogeneity in assessment tools for mood/anxiety outcomes and limited adjustment for confounders weaken causal claims. The strongest association (prior psychiatric history) is clinically meaningful, while other RRs are modest; none exceed 2 except prior psychiatric history. Sensitivity analyses suggested less robust associations for tumor grade, surgery extent, socioeconomic factors, and social support.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These factors can inform targeted screening in oncology clinics, prioritizing patients with prior psychiatric illness, advanced disease, multiple comorbidities, or social vulnerabilities. Routine screening should still be universal given the high baseline prevalence, but high-risk groups may warrant earlier or more frequent assessment.

item.title: [17] Non-hormonal management of menopause symptoms-the statement of the European Society of Gynecology.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This guideline from the European Society of Gynecology reviews non-hormonal interventions for menopausal symptoms (vasomotor symptoms, sleep disturbance, mood disorders, genitourinary syndrome of menopause) in women who decline or cannot use menopausal hormone therapy, synthesizing evidence from clinical guidelines, systematic reviews, RCTs, and primary studies.
FINDINGS: Lifestyle modification is foundational. Among drugs, SSRIs/SNRIs, gabapentin, clonidine, oxybutynin, and pregabalin show varying efficacy for vasomotor symptoms; neurokinin-3 receptor antagonists (fezolinetant, elinzanetant) have the strongest evidence. Psychological therapies (CBT, hypnosis) reduce symptom-related distress and improve sleep and quality of life. For GSM, lubricants/moisturizers and hyaluronic acid are beneficial; vaginal laser therapy lacks supportive evidence.
INTERPRETATION: The guideline is a consensus statement based on structured literature review rather than a formal systematic review or meta-analysis, so the strength of evidence varies widely across interventions. Neurokinin receptor antagonists have the most robust RCT support, while evidence for complementary therapies is moderate to limited. The guideline does not quantify effect sizes or confidence intervals, limiting assessment of clinical significance. External validity is constrained by selective inclusion of studies and lack of patient-representative populations.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Clinicians can consider non-hormonal options tailored to symptom profile and patient preference, prioritizing neurokinin antagonists for vasomotor symptoms and moisturizers for GSM, while recognizing that evidence quality is uneven and some recommendations are based on low-certainty data.

item.title: [15] Cost-effectiveness of psychedelic-assisted therapies for depression and post-traumatic stress disorder: A systematic review.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: Psychedelic-assisted therapies (MDMA and psilocybin) show promise for depression and PTSD but are resource-intensive. This systematic review (PRISMA 2020) evaluated their cost-effectiveness compared to standard care, focusing on high-income settings.
FINDINGS: Seven studies were included (5 MDMA-AT for PTSD, 2 psilocybin-assisted therapy [PAT] for treatment-resistant depression [TRD]). All used high-quality economic models. MDMA-AT was generally cost-effective vs. standard care (ICERs below common willingness-to-pay thresholds). Evidence for PAT was limited and mixed, with no clear cost-effectiveness conclusion.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence for MDMA-AT in PTSD is relatively robust, suggesting potential economic value in high-income contexts. However, the PAT evidence base is too small to draw firm conclusions. Limitations include reliance on modeled data (no real-world cost studies), lack of diversity in settings (all high-income), and heterogeneity in model structures. Funding sources were not reported, which may introduce bias.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: MDMA-assisted therapy for PTSD may offer cost-effective benefits in high-income settings, but adoption should await confirmatory real-world studies. PAT for TRD remains experimental from both clinical and economic perspectives. Clinicians should monitor emerging economic evaluations before advocating for resource allocation.

item.title: [14] Intolerance of Uncertainty Among US and Canadian Young Adults Attending College 1992-2023: A Meta-Analysis.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study examined whether intolerance of uncertainty (IU)—difficulty enduring ambiguous situations—has increased among US and Canadian college students from 1992 to 2023, using a meta-analysis of 137 studies with 37,298 participants.
FINDINGS: Mean long-form IU scores rose by 0.66 points annually (95% CI, 0.47–0.84) on a 27–135 scale, and short-form IU scores rose by 0.60 points annually (95% CI, 0.43–0.76) on a 12–60 scale. Standardized mean IU increased by 0.04 SD per year overall, with a threefold acceleration after 2012 (0.06 SD/year vs. 0.02 SD/year pre-2012).
INTERPRETATION: The evidence is moderate-to-high in internal validity (preregistered, MOOSE-guided, large sample, sensitivity analyses), but external validity is limited to North American undergraduates, mostly female. The effect size is small per year but cumulative over decades; whether this reflects a true rise in clinical anxiety or measurement artifacts remains uncertain. Funding sources were not reported.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: The findings suggest growing intolerance of uncertainty among college students, particularly since 2012, which may inform anxiety prevention strategies; however, the clinical impact of these small annual shifts is unclear and warrants longitudinal outcome studies.

item.title: [13] Cost-Effectiveness of Alcohol Use Disorder Treatment for Alcohol-Associated Liver Disease.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study used a Markov model to assess whether naltrexone plus a 16-week course of combined behavioral intervention (CBI) for alcohol use disorder (AUD) is cost-effective in preventing cirrhosis progression among 45-year-old patients with alcohol-associated liver disease (ALD) at stage F3 fibrosis, compared with no treatment.
FINDINGS: Without treatment, the model projected 61 % liver-related mortality, 88 % compensated cirrhosis, 66 % decompensated cirrhosis, and lifetime cost of $79 799 per person. With treatment, mortality fell to 58 %, compensated cirrhosis to 87 %, decompensated cirrhosis to 62 %, and lifetime cost to $78 673, while quality-adjusted life-years (QALYs) increased. The treatment strategy dominated (lower cost, higher QALYs) and remained cost-effective in sensitivity analyses across relapse rates up to 100 % and adherence > 0 %, and in scenario analyses starting at F2 and F1 fibrosis stages.
INTERPRETATION: The economic model suggests that adding naltrexone and CBI to usual care for ALD at F3 fibrosis is cost-saving and improves outcomes versus no AUD treatment. Strengths include extensive sensitivity and scenario analyses showing robustness. However, the analysis is based on a simulated cohort and relies on multiple assumptions about treatment adherence, relapse rates, and costs; real-world effectiveness and adherence may differ. Prospective trials are needed to validate these projections.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: If confirmed in practice, early pharmacotherapy plus behavioral intervention for AUD in ALD could reduce cirrhosis progression and health care costs; clinicians should consider integrating MAUD and CBI into routine care for patients with ALD, even at early fibrosis stages.

item.title: [12] Neuroscience-informed psychoeducation for autism.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This chapter proposes a neuroscience-informed psychoeducation framework (NIPE-fA) for autism spectrum disorder (ASD), integrating developmental neuroscience with psychoeducational practices. It targets modifiable neural connectivity and experience-dependent neuroplasticity, advocating the ECCC model (Early, Continuous, Comprehensive, Context-based intervention) as a translational approach to optimize brain and behavioral outcomes in ASD.
FINDINGS: The chapter synthesizes theoretical and empirical evidence to argue that targeted environmental inputs (e.g., parent-mediated interventions) may influence early brain development, connectivity patterns, and social brain networks in ASD. It emphasizes contextual factors affecting treatment adherence and effectiveness, positioning NIPE-fA as a bridge between neuroscience and clinical practice.
INTERPRETATION: As a narrative review without original empirical data, this work is exploratory and lacks quantitative effect sizes, confidence intervals, or statistical comparisons. Its strength lies in conceptual integration, but the absence of experimental validation limits confidence in clinical recommendations. The proposed framework remains theoretical, with uncertain generalizability to routine care pending empirical testing.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: This framework offers a novel perspective on ASD intervention but does not yet provide actionable evidence to change practice. Clinicians may find the ECCC model conceptually useful, but its implementation should be approached cautiously until supported by rigorous trials.

item.title: [10] Treatment completion and quality of life in inpatient alcohol treatment: a secondary observational analysis within a randomized controlled trial in Interior Alaska.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study examined whether treatment completion in long-term inpatient alcohol treatment improves quality of life (QoL) at six months, using data from a randomized controlled trial (Transitions to Recovery) in Interior Alaska. It tested whether baseline psychosocial functioning predicted completion and whether completers had better QoL outcomes.
FINDINGS: No significant baseline differences in psychosocial functioning were found between treatment completers and non-completers. At six months, completers had higher EQ-5D-5L utility scores than non-completers (0.81 vs. 0.73, p = 0.04), with fewer problems in mobility and usual activities, but not in anxiety/depression. The association was attenuated and became non-significant after covariate adjustment.
INTERPRETATION: The study’s internal validity is limited by the lack of baseline QoL data, making it impossible to determine whether pre-existing physical functioning differences drove completion or resulted from it. The observed association is likely confounded and not robust to adjustment. The findings are preliminary and should not be interpreted as causal. The economic projection (0.40–0.75 QALYs over 5–10 years) assumes sustained benefit without empirical support.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence does not support the claim that inpatient alcohol treatment completion improves QoL, particularly in mental health domains. Clinicians should not assume treatment completion leads to better QoL without further research.

item.title: [9] Be a Mom implementation study protocol: integrating a universal digital intervention for postpartum depression into the Portuguese national health service.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study is a protocol for implementing *Be a Mom*, a self-guided internet-delivered cognitive behavioural therapy (iCBT) intervention for postpartum depression, within the Portuguese National Health Service (SNS). It aims to evaluate the feasibility and effectiveness of integrating this digital intervention into routine maternal care, targeting postpartum women across 20 health units over 18 months.
FINDINGS: The study will use a mixed-methods approach guided by the PRISM framework to assess implementation outcomes (reach, effectiveness, adoption, and implementation) at patient, provider, and setting levels. Qualitative thematic analysis will explore contextual factors influencing adoption. While efficacy and cost-effectiveness of *Be a Mom* have been demonstrated in prior studies, this protocol focuses on real-world implementation rather than clinical outcomes.
INTERPRETATION: As a protocol, this study has not yet produced results, so no findings are available to interpret. The design is robust in its mixed-methods approach and use of a recognised implementation framework (PRISM), which may enhance generalisability if successful. However, the lack of comparator groups or randomisation limits causal inference. External validity will depend on the representativeness of the 20 participating health units and the engagement of postpartum women and providers.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: This study could inform future scale-up of digital mental health interventions in public health systems, but no clinical changes should be made until implementation outcomes and effectiveness data are available. Clinicians should monitor for emerging evidence from this study to guide adoption of *Be a Mom* in routine care.

item.title: [9] Development of PRECISE, a Data-Driven Personalized Suicide Prevention Intervention: Protocol for an Intervention Refinement Pilot and Randomized Controlled Trial.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study aims to refine and pilot-test PRECISE, an 8-week, ecological momentary assessment (EMA)-informed, idiographically tailored adjunctive treatment for adults with active suicidal ideation, addressing the heterogeneity of suicidal thoughts and behaviors (STBs) and the resource-intensive nature of standard dialectical behavior therapy (DBT). The protocol outlines a randomized pilot (aim 1) and a larger randomized controlled trial (aim 2) comparing high- vs. low-intensity personalization schedules in PRECISE.
FINDINGS: Aim 1 involves a small pilot (n=10, 5 per arm) to test feasibility and acceptability of PRECISE, while aim 2 plans to randomize 60 adults with active suicidal ideation to high-intensity (weekly idiographic model updates) or low-intensity (single model after 2-week EMA burst) personalization. Primary outcomes include usability, retention, EMA adherence, acceptability, and fidelity; secondary outcomes will explore trajectories of suicidal ideation and mediation models linking emotion regulation to STBs. As of November 9, 2026, 7 participants had been enrolled, with full enrollment and data collection expected by March 2030.
INTERPRETATION: This is a protocol for an ongoing randomized trial, so no results are available yet. The study design is rigorous, with randomization and a clear focus on feasibility and preliminary efficacy. However, the small pilot sample and lack of published outcomes limit conclusions. The idiographic approach is innovative but requires validation in larger, diverse populations to assess generalizability and clinical utility. The funding source and trial registration enhance transparency, but the long timeline and early recruitment stage mean clinical relevance remains uncertain until results are published.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: At this stage, PRECISE is a promising but unproven intervention. Clinicians should monitor future publications for preliminary efficacy data before considering adoption. The personalized approach may eventually offer a more efficient alternative to standard DBT, but further evidence is needed.

item.title: [7] Atomoxetine and risk of Alzheimer's disease in older adults.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This non-concurrent prospective cohort study (emulating a target trial) investigated whether atomoxetine initiation in older adults (Medicare beneficiaries, 2007–2023) reduces the 5- or 10-year risk of Alzheimer’s disease (AD) compared to non-initiation, addressing conflicting preclinical and small RCT evidence suggesting potential disease-modifying effects.
FINDINGS: The study included 70,367 person-trials (mean age ≥70 years; 59.5% female; 86.7% non-Hispanic White). Atomoxetine initiation was **not associated** with 5-year (RR ~1.0, 95% CI not reported) or 10-year AD risk versus non-initiation. However, it was linked to a **lower risk of AD-free death** at 5 years (RR and RD not specified). In subgroup analyses, atomoxetine was associated with **lower 5-year AD risk and AD-free death** among individuals with depression (effect sizes not quantified in the abstract).
INTERPRETATION: The evidence suggests no overall reduction in AD risk with atomoxetine, but a potential benefit in depressed older adults warrants cautious interpretation due to unquantified effect sizes and subgroup analyses. Strengths include the large, real-world cohort and validated AD ascertainment, but limitations include residual confounding (e.g., indication bias, unmeasured comorbidities), lack of randomization, and no adjustment for multiple comparisons in subgroup analyses. The clinical significance of the "AD-free death" finding is unclear without effect sizes.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Atomoxetine cannot be recommended for AD prevention in older adults based on this study. Further research is needed to clarify the observed association in depressed patients, ideally via randomized trials or robustly adjusted observational designs. Clinicians should not alter prescribing practices for AD prevention until confirmatory evidence emerges.

item.title: [7] Assessing nurses performance on a violence risk assessment instrument paired with structured intervention guidelines to prevent aggression.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study examines whether an Entrustable Professional Activities (EPA) framework can support forensic mental health nurses in learning and applying the Dynamic Appraisal of Situational Aggression (DASA) paired with a structured Aggression Prevention Protocol (APP) to reduce aggression in secure settings. The research uses simulation-based trials with thematic analysis of focus group data to assess the EPA framework’s effectiveness in teaching and evaluating these skills.
FINDINGS: Participants reported that the EPA framework helped structure assessment conversations, supported reflective learning, and clarified practice expectations. They valued strengths-based feedback and self-reflection opportunities, suggesting the framework could enhance risk assessment and aggression prevention practices. No quantitative outcomes (e.g., aggression rates, effect sizes) were reported.
INTERPRETATION: This is a qualitative, simulation-based study with no comparator or blinding, limiting internal validity. Thematic analysis suggests perceived benefits, but the absence of measurable outcomes (e.g., aggression reduction, inter-rater reliability) and reliance on self-reported feedback from a small, non-randomized sample weakens confidence in generalizability. The study highlights potential for EPAs in training but does not establish clinical effectiveness.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: The EPA framework may offer a structured approach to teaching DASA + APP, but its impact on patient outcomes or nursing performance in real-world settings remains unproven. Further research with controlled designs and objective outcomes is needed before recommending adoption in routine practice.

item.title: [7] Neuroscience-informed psychoeducation for borderline and other personality disorders: From emotion dysregulation to adaptive self-regulation.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This narrative review examines whether neuroscience-informed psychoeducation (NIPE) can improve outcomes for patients with borderline personality disorder (BPD) and other personality disorders by translating neurobiological findings into patient-friendly education. It synthesizes current diagnostic challenges, the role of psychoeducation, and emerging neuroimaging evidence to guide clinical practice.
FINDINGS: The chapter highlights that psychoeducation is a core component of all evidence-based treatments for BPD and that integrating neuroscience concepts—such as emotion dysregulation and neural circuit dysfunction—can enhance patient understanding and self-management. While specific quantitative outcomes are not reported, the review emphasizes that high-quality educational resources and disorder disclosure are associated with improved healthcare engagement and outcomes. fMRI studies are cited as supporting the neurobiological basis of BPD, but no effect sizes, confidence intervals, or p-values are provided.
INTERPRETATION: As a narrative review, this paper provides a conceptual framework rather than empirical evidence. Its strength lies in integrating neurobiological insights with clinical psychoeducation strategies, but it lacks rigorous study design, quantitative data, or systematic evidence appraisal. The absence of effect sizes or controlled comparisons limits the ability to assess clinical significance. The discussion is largely theoretical, and generalizability depends on how well neuroscience concepts can be translated into accessible psychoeducation in real-world settings.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: This review supports the continued use of psychoeducation in BPD care and suggests that incorporating neuroscience-informed explanations may enhance patient engagement and self-regulation. However, it does not provide actionable data to change practice beyond what is already recommended in evidence-based guidelines. Clinicians may consider piloting NIPE approaches but should await controlled trials to determine whether such strategies yield measurable improvements in symptoms or functioning.

item.title: [6] Pharmacologic Rationale and Clinical Evidence for Treatments that Target Monoamine Dysregulation in Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder: A Narrative Review.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This narrative review examines pharmacological treatments for PTSD that target monoamine dysregulation (norepinephrine, serotonin, dopamine), summarizing mechanisms, efficacy, and safety of on-label (sertraline, paroxetine) and off-label agents. It focuses on how monoamine system modulation relates to PTSD symptom clusters and fear/stress/reward processes.
FINDINGS: The review highlights that sertraline and paroxetine have the strongest evidence among approved treatments, with off-label venlafaxine also supported. Atypical antipsychotics like risperidone and brexpiprazole have been studied in larger samples but show mixed efficacy. The review emphasizes that drug selection may be guided by monoamine receptor profiles to match symptom domains.
INTERPRETATION: As a narrative review without systematic methods or quantitative synthesis, the strength of evidence is limited by selection bias and lack of standardized assessment. The conclusions rely on summarizing existing studies rather than meta-analytic pooling. While mechanistic rationale is plausible, clinical efficacy claims are largely based on aggregated trial data without effect sizes or direct comparisons. The review does not quantify adverse effects or long-term outcomes.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current practice should still prioritize SSRIs (sertraline/paroxetine) as first-line pharmacotherapy for PTSD, with venlafaxine as a reasonable off-label alternative. Atypical antipsychotics may be considered cautiously in select cases, but evidence is inconsistent and side effects are significant. This review supports a rational, mechanism-informed approach to drug choice but does not change standard treatment guidelines.

item.title: [37] Lithium for Suicide Prevention: Umbrella Review and Meta-Analysis.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study re-examines the long-standing clinical question of whether lithium reduces suicide-related outcomes in psychiatric patients by synthesizing contemporary randomized evidence. It updates prior meta-analyses with a comprehensive search and rigorous GRADE assessment to clarify lithium’s preventive effects.
FINDINGS: Across 22 randomized strata (n=3,675), lithium showed a non-significant pooled odds ratio for completed suicide (OR=0.39, 95% CI 0.15–1.00; I²=0%). A Peto sensitivity analysis reached significance (OR=0.42, 95% CI 0.18–0.98), but excluding the most influential trial attenuated the effect (OR=0.43, 95% CI 0.13–1.40). A subgroup of mixed mood-disorder trials suggested benefit (OR=0.25, 95% CI 0.07–0.90). No consistent effects were found for suicide attempts, self-harm, all-cause mortality, or composite events. Treatment discontinuation favored lithium over placebo but not over active comparators. GRADE certainty was low to very low.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is fragile: the completed-suicide signal is sparse, highly sensitive to analytic choices, and driven by a small number of events. The lack of effect across related outcomes and low GRADE ratings mean conclusions remain tentative. Pragmatic trials with prespecified suicide outcomes and balanced clinical contact are needed before practice changes.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Lithium may still be considered for suicide prevention on clinical grounds, but the current evidence does not mandate its use solely for suicide prevention. Clinicians should weigh benefits against discontinuation risks and monitor closely.

item.title: [20] GLP-1 Receptor Agonists in Psychotic Disorders: Mechanistic Convergence and Therapeutic Implications for Brain and Metabolic Health.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review examined whether glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) can improve brain and metabolic health in people with psychotic disorders. The authors synthesized preclinical and early clinical evidence to assess mechanistic plausibility and therapeutic potential.
FINDINGS: Preclinical studies suggest GLP-1RAs may modulate glucose homeostasis, gut-brain signaling, inflammation, redox balance, mitochondrial function, and reward pathways. In clinical trials, GLP-1RAs consistently reduced antipsychotic-associated weight gain and improved cardiometabolic outcomes (e.g., body weight, HbA1c), though data on psychotic symptoms, cognition, or functioning remain inconsistent. Evidence for reducing alcohol or nicotine use is suggestive but inconclusive. Most trials were small, short-term, and heterogeneous in design and dosing.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is preliminary and limited by small samples, short follow-up, and heterogeneity. While the mechanistic rationale is biologically plausible and metabolic benefits are supported, effects on core psychotic symptoms or functioning are unproven. The cardiometabolic benefits are clinically meaningful for a high-risk population, but broader neuropsychiatric claims require larger, longer, and more rigorous trials with mechanistic endpoints.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: GLP-1RAs can be considered for managing antipsychotic-induced weight gain and cardiometabolic risk in patients with psychotic disorders. Routine use for psychotic symptoms, cognition, or substance use is not yet supported. Clinicians should monitor metabolic parameters and remain cautious about extrapolating benefits beyond weight and metabolic outcomes.

item.title: [15] Experiences of late-diagnosed autistic women: a qualitative systematic review and meta-synthesis protocol.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This is a protocol for a qualitative systematic review and meta-synthesis (JBI meta-aggregation) examining the lived experiences, diagnostic journeys, and post-diagnostic adaptation of late-diagnosed autistic women, a group often overlooked due to gender disparities in autism identification and diagnostic biases. The review will synthesize qualitative and mixed-methods studies published up to March 2027.
FINDINGS: The review will include peer-reviewed qualitative or mixed-methods studies focusing on autistic women diagnosed in adolescence or adulthood, with no restrictions on gender identity. Two independent reviewers will conduct study selection, data extraction, and quality appraisal using the JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist, and synthesize findings using a three-step meta-aggregation approach. Confidence in the synthesized findings will be assessed using the ConQual tool. The formal literature search is planned to commence in January 2027.
INTERPRETATION: As this is a protocol, no results are available yet. The planned methodology (JBI meta-aggregation, PRISMA-P compliant, dual independent review, and ConQual assessment) suggests a rigorous approach to synthesizing qualitative evidence. However, the review's utility will depend on the breadth and quality of included studies, which are not yet known. The focus on late-diagnosed autistic women addresses an important gap in the literature, but generalizability may be limited by the heterogeneity of qualitative studies and the inclusion of diverse gender identities.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: This review could provide valuable insights into the diagnostic and post-diagnostic experiences of late-diagnosed autistic women, potentially informing clinical practice and support strategies. However, as the review is still in the protocol stage, no immediate changes to clinical practice are warranted. Clinicians should remain aware of the potential for delayed or missed diagnoses in autistic women and consider the unique challenges they may face.

item.title: [10] Psychiatric Relapse After First-Trimester Antipsychotic Discontinuation in Pregnant Women with Schizophrenia: A Nationwide Cohort Study in South Korea.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This nationwide cohort study in South Korea examined whether discontinuing antipsychotics in the first trimester of pregnancy increases relapse risk in women with schizophrenia, using propensity score–weighted comparisons and registry data.
FINDINGS: Among 1,790 eligible episodes (1,205 discontinuation vs 585 continuation), first-trimester discontinuation was linked to a higher relapse risk (adjusted hazard ratio 2.05, 95 % CI 1.47–2.87). The risk increase was pronounced in women with a recent schizophrenia diagnosis (aHR 2.80, 95 % CI 1.93–4.04) but not in those with a recent bipolar disorder diagnosis (aHR 0.35, 95 % CI 0.11–1.10).
INTERPRETATION: The study provides moderate-strength evidence that first-trimester discontinuation roughly doubles relapse risk in pregnant women with schizophrenia, especially when the diagnosis is recent. Limitations include reliance on administrative codes for relapse and diagnosis, potential residual confounding, and lack of data on medication adherence or dose changes. The effect size is statistically robust but clinical significance depends on baseline relapse risk and patient preferences.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Clinicians should weigh the relapse risk against potential fetal exposure when considering first-trimester antipsychotic discontinuation in women with schizophrenia; careful monitoring or gradual tapering may be prudent, particularly for those with recent schizophrenia diagnoses.

item.title: [10] A Comprehensive Intervention to Enhance Treatment Engagement and Retention Following Nonfatal Opioid Overdose: Protocol for a Single-Arm Prospective Feasibility Study.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study assessed the feasibility and acceptability of a 12-week telehealth-enabled bundled intervention (buprenorphine, telehealth physician visits, telehealth peer support, and facilitated linkage to community resources) to improve treatment engagement and retention among adults with opioid use disorder (OUD) and a recent nonfatal opioid overdose after hospital discharge. This single-arm prospective feasibility study (R61 phase) aimed to inform a future randomized controlled trial (R33 phase).
FINDINGS: The study enrolled 30 participants, with 24 completing the 12-week intervention (retention rate 80%). Feasibility was measured against a benchmark of ≥70% retention at 3 months, which was met. Acceptability was assessed via patient satisfaction and credibility/expectancy scores, though specific values were not reported. Secondary outcomes included mental health, craving, repeat overdose, and emergency department revisits/readmissions, with results pending publication in January 2027.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence is preliminary and limited by the single-arm design, lack of a control group, and small sample size, which preclude causal inferences about effectiveness. The high retention rate (80%) suggests feasibility and acceptability, but the absence of comparative data (e.g., against standard care) and unblinded assessments may introduce bias. The study’s strengths include its structured intervention and clear feasibility benchmarks. However, the lack of reported secondary outcomes and reliance on descriptive analysis limit interpretability. The upcoming R33 phase (RCT) will be critical to determine clinical efficacy.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: This study does not yet provide evidence to change practice but establishes feasibility for a bundled telehealth intervention in a high-risk population. Clinicians should await results from the R33 phase before considering adoption, as current findings only support the intervention’s acceptability and retention potential, not its superiority over standard care.

item.title: [10] Clinical instability, inflammatory markers, and mortality in schizophrenia spectrum disorders: A large real-world cohort study.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This large retrospective cohort study using TriNetX electronic health records examined whether clinical instability in schizophrenia spectrum disorders (SSD) is associated with elevated inflammatory markers and worse outcomes, including mortality. The study compared patients with higher severity SSD (HS-SSD) to those with lower severity SSD (LS-SSD) using propensity score matching.
FINDINGS: The cohort included 140,862 patients per group. All-cause mortality was higher in HS-SSD than LS-SSD (12.38% vs 11.58%; risk ratio [RR] 1.068, 95% CI 1.047–1.090; hazard ratio 1.096, 95% CI 1.073–1.119). Elevated inflammatory markers (C-reactive protein ≥3.0 mg/L and/or lactate dehydrogenase ≥220 U/L) were also more common in HS-SSD (12.55% vs 11.30%; RR 1.110, 95% CI 1.086–1.135; P < .001). Subsequent hospitalization was more frequent in HS-SSD (0.56% vs 0.02%), reflecting the cohort definition. Differences in cardiometabolic measures (e.g., glycated hemoglobin, LDL cholesterol) were negligible (Cohen d ≤ 0.07).
INTERPRETATION: The study provides robust real-world evidence linking clinical instability in SSD to higher mortality and elevated inflammatory markers, with strong internal validity due to the large sample size and propensity score matching. However, the retrospective design and reliance on proxy indicators of instability limit causal inference. The negligible differences in cardiometabolic measures suggest that inflammation may operate independently of metabolic dysregulation in this context. The effect sizes, while statistically significant, are modest and may not translate into immediate clinical changes.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These findings suggest that monitoring inflammatory markers in patients with SSD and high clinical instability could be considered, though routine practice changes are not yet justified. Further research is needed to determine whether targeting inflammation improves outcomes in this subgroup.

item.title: [9] Self-guided web-based mindfulness and skills-based distress reduction training versus treatment as usual optimised in patients with cancer (Reduct): a multicentre, parallel-group, randomised controlled trial.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The trial tested whether a 16-week self-guided web-based mindfulness and skills-based distress-reduction programme reduced anxiety and depression symptoms more than optimised treatment-as-usual (TAU-O) in recently diagnosed or progressing cancer patients with elevated distress, using a multicentre RCT design across eight German university hospitals.
FINDINGS: 561 adults (18–65 years) were randomised (intervention n=281, control n=280). At 16 weeks, HADS total score fell from 18.59 to 13.34 in the intervention group and from 19.60 to 15.13 in controls; adjusted between-group difference −1.00 (95 % CI −2.09 to 0.09; p=0.073). Secondary outcomes showed significantly greater reductions in anxiety (−1.19, 95 % CI −2.06 to −0.32) and increases in self-efficacy (0.44, 95 % CI 0.18 to 0.70).
INTERPRETATION: The trial was well-powered and conducted across multiple centres, but the primary outcome did not reach statistical significance, indicating no clear superiority of the web-based intervention over TAU-O for overall distress. The small but statistically significant improvements in anxiety and self-efficacy suggest potential adjunctive benefits, though effect sizes are modest and unblinded self-report measures may inflate them. The recruitment pause and cyberattack introduce minor feasibility concerns without obvious bias.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: The intervention does not currently warrant replacement of standard psychosocial oncology care for distress reduction, but could be considered as an adjunct in stepped-care models, particularly for patients with prominent anxiety. Clinicians should monitor for modest gains rather than expecting large effects.

item.title: [8] Mapping the shared genetic architecture between anorexia nervosa and metabolomic biomarkers.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This large-scale genomic study investigated whether anorexia nervosa (AN) shares genetic architecture with 249 circulating metabolomic biomarkers, aiming to clarify AN’s metabolic underpinnings and identify potential treatment targets. Using summary-level data from genome-wide association studies (GWAS), the authors assessed genetic correlations, causal links, and tissue-specific gene expression.
FINDINGS: Significant genetic correlations were found between AN and 142 metabolomic biomarkers, with correlations opposite in direction to those seen for BMI and type 2 diabetes (e.g., rs < −0.94). Shared variants implicated lipid-related pathways, developmental growth, and inflammation, with gene expression enriched in brain, internal organs, and female reproductive tissues. Bidirectional associations between AN and metabolomic biomarkers appeared to act through BMI.
INTERPRETATION: This is a high-quality GWAS-based study leveraging large genomic datasets, providing robust evidence of shared genetic architecture between AN and systemic metabolism. Limitations include reliance on summary statistics (no individual-level data), potential population stratification, and unclear clinical translation of genetic correlations. The effect sizes are strong at the genetic level but do not directly translate to clinical outcomes or treatment decisions.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These findings support a metabo-psychiatric model of AN and highlight lipid and inflammatory pathways as potential targets for future research, but they do not yet justify changes in clinical practice. Monitoring metabolomic profiles may become relevant in precision medicine, but current evidence is preliminary.

item.title: [7] Impact of nutritional factors on the pharmacokinetics of ADHD medication - a systematic review.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review examined how nutritional factors (e.g., food intake, alcohol) influence the pharmacokinetics of ADHD medications (stimulants and non-stimulants) in humans. The clinical question is whether dietary or alcohol interactions alter drug absorption, metabolism, or exposure, potentially affecting efficacy and tolerability. The review included 33 clinical studies, mostly small, single-dose pharmacokinetic studies in healthy adults, with limited data in patients with ADHD or under steady-state conditions.
FINDINGS: Most ADHD medications showed pharmacokinetic changes with food intake, primarily affecting the *rate* (e.g., delayed tmax, altered Cmax) rather than the *extent* (e.g., total AUC) of absorption. Modified-release formulations exhibited greater variability in exposure profiles (e.g., early exposure, tmax, Cmax) despite relatively preserved AUC. Alcohol co-administration with methylphenidate increased exposure and led to the formation of ethylphenidate. Evidence for non-stimulants (e.g., extended-release clonidine, viloxazine) was minimal, with only one eligible study per drug.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is weak due to small sample sizes, reliance on healthy volunteers, and lack of steady-state or patient-focused studies. While the findings suggest food and alcohol can meaningfully alter drug exposure—particularly for methylphenidate—the clinical relevance of these pharmacokinetic changes remains uncertain. The review highlights a critical gap in translational research: whether these pharmacokinetic shifts translate into clinically meaningful differences in efficacy, side effects, or dosing requirements. The conclusions about clinical significance are largely inferential rather than empirically supported.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence supports cautious patient counseling about consistent dosing conditions (e.g., with or without food) to minimize pharmacokinetic variability, especially for modified-release formulations. Alcohol use with methylphenidate may warrant stronger warnings due to increased exposure and potential toxicity risk. However, routine dose adjustments based solely on nutritional factors are not yet justified due to insufficient clinical outcome data.

item.title: [6] Redevelopment and validation of clinical risk assessment models for suicide in schizophrenia-spectrum disorders and bipolar disorder (OxMIS2).
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study redeveloped and externally validated diagnosis-specific suicide risk prediction models (OxMIS2) for individuals with schizophrenia-spectrum disorders (SCZS) and bipolar disorder (BIP) using Swedish and Finnish national registers. The aim was to improve clinical decision-making for suicide risk assessment in these high-risk populations.
FINDINGS: The Swedish derivation cohorts included 48,373 individuals with SCZS (422 suicides, 0.9%) and 61,684 with BIP (357 suicides, 0.6%). External validation in Finland included 52,117 and 30,444 patients, respectively, with suicide proportions of 0.7% and 0.5%. The final models included 11 predictors for SCZS (AUC 0.69, 95% CI 0.67–0.72) and 9 for BIP (AUC 0.81, 95% CI 0.79–0.83). External validation yielded AUCs of 0.68 (SCZS) and 0.77 (BIP), with good calibration. Decision curve analysis suggested net benefit over treat-all or treat-none strategies at lower risk thresholds.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence is moderate-strength, based on large, well-defined national cohorts with external validation. Discrimination is moderate for SCZS and good for BIP, but absolute risk of suicide remains low (≤0.9%), limiting clinical impact. The models’ calibration and net benefit in decision curve analysis support potential utility, though real-world implementation studies are needed to confirm impact on patient outcomes and resource allocation.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: OxMIS2 may assist in structured suicide risk assessment for SCZS and BIP, particularly to guide low-intensity interventions (e.g., enhanced follow-up, safety planning). However, clinicians should avoid over-reliance on risk scores given modest discrimination and low base rates of suicide.

item.title: [6] Roots to Thrive risk and readiness assessment: a practice-based intake and decision-support framework for psychedelic-assisted therapy.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study describes the development of a trauma-informed, context-responsive readiness and risk assessment framework for psychedelic-assisted therapy (PaT) in community-based settings, addressing limitations of trial-derived intake approaches that prioritise biomedical exclusion over relational, cultural, and environmental factors.
FINDINGS: The framework was iteratively refined through multi-year practice-based quality improvement in a community PaT programme and a university-based education setting. It integrates biomedical, psychological, relational, cultural, ecological, and transpersonal domains to guide intake decisions on fit, readiness, and risk, with reported benefits including clearer readiness articulation, shared interdisciplinary language, and improved alignment between intake practices and real-world PaT delivery.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence is preliminary and practice-based, lacking psychometric validation or comparative data. Strengths include its trauma-informed, context-responsive design and iterative refinement in real-world settings. However, generalisability is limited by its single-service context and absence of formal validation. The framework’s utility in improving clinical outcomes remains unproven, and its focus on readiness over exclusion may not address all safety concerns.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: This framework may aid transparent intake decision-making and governance in community PaT but should be viewed as a preliminary tool pending psychometric validation and broader evaluation. Clinicians should use it cautiously, recognising its unvalidated status and the need for further evidence.

item.title: [15] [Development of an optimal acupuncture-moxibustion treatment protocol for perimenopausal insomnia].
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review with network meta-analysis and multi-criteria decision-making (MCDM) evaluated 32 RCTs (n≈2,500) comparing 19 acupuncture-moxibustion protocols plus 3 controls for perimenopausal insomnia, ranking interventions by total effective rate, PSQI, modified KMI, and treatment frequency.
FINDINGS: Network meta-analysis showed highest SUCRA rankings for depression-relieving acupuncture + western medication (total effective rate SUCRA 0.76; PSQI 0.93) and back-shu acupuncture + warming needle (total effective rate 0.75; PSQI 0.84; KMI 0.84). MCDM ranked back-shu + warming needle first for combined efficacy and cost (TOPSIS closeness 0.7808; VIKOR Q=0).
INTERPRETATION: Evidence is low-certainty due to methodological heterogeneity, lack of preregistered protocols, and high risk of bias in included Chinese RCTs. SUCRA values reflect relative ranking within a limited evidence base rather than clinically meaningful effect sizes; no absolute effect estimates or confidence intervals are reported. The MCDM ranking integrates cost but relies on arbitrary weighting and may not generalize beyond the studied protocols.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current data do not justify changing practice; back-shu + warming needle may be considered an option but should be compared head-to-head against guideline-recommended treatments (e.g., CBT-I, hormone therapy) in adequately powered, high-quality RCTs with patient-centered outcomes.

item.title: [11] Sustainability of Treatment Success 5 Years after Exposure-Based Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy for Anxiety Disorders.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This multicenter clinical trial assessed whether gains from exposure-based cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) for anxiety disorders are sustained five years after treatment, addressing a gap in long-term outcome data for routine psychiatric care.
FINDINGS: Of 355 patients (58% follow-up), improvements in anxiety symptoms and psychosocial functioning seen immediately post-treatment and at 6 months were largely maintained at 5 years. No significant differences were found between intensified vs. non-intensified exposure schedules. Overall remission rates remained stable (6 months: ~70%; 5 years: ~68%), with 4.9% experiencing reliable relapse and 6.5% reliable new remission. Only 36.6% sought additional treatment, most commonly for depression (64.2%) or anxiety (60.5%), though only 6.0% sought further treatment *exclusively* for anxiety. Additional treatment during follow-up correlated with higher symptom severity across all time points.
INTERPRETATION: The study provides moderate-quality longitudinal evidence (58% follow-up, no attrition analysis) suggesting durable benefits of exposure-based CBT for most patients. Strengths include a large sample, high treatment fidelity, and repeated-measures design. However, selection bias (58% retention) and lack of a control group limit causal inference. The small relapse/new remission rates (4.9–6.5%) suggest clinical stability for most, but the association between additional treatment and higher severity warrants caution—it may reflect residual symptomatology rather than treatment failure. External validity is reasonable for patients completing exposure-based CBT in specialized settings.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These findings support the long-term effectiveness of exposure-based CBT for anxiety disorders, with most patients remaining stable without further treatment. Clinicians can reassure patients about sustained benefits but should monitor those with residual symptoms, as they may require additional support. Further research is needed to optimize outcomes for non-remitters.

item.title: [10] Analysis of the placebo response model and its influencing factors in attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder: a model-based meta-analysis.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study used a model-based meta-analysis (MBMA) of 79 placebo-controlled randomized clinical trials (RCTs) to quantify the longitudinal trajectory of the placebo response in ADHD, identify trial- and patient-level predictors, and compare pediatric vs. adult populations to inform future trial design.
FINDINGS: Placebo responses on ADHD-RS and CGI-S followed non-linear trajectories, plateauing at ~6 weeks (ADHD-RS) and ~10 weeks (CGI-S). Larger sample sizes, recent trials, multicenter designs, industry sponsorship, and use of stimulant comparators were associated with higher placebo responses. Pediatric and adult placebo trajectories were similar in shape and magnitude.
INTERPRETATION: The MBMA leverages a large dataset and advanced modeling, strengthening internal validity for describing placebo dynamics. However, as an aggregate analysis, it cannot infer causality for predictors and may be confounded by unmeasured trial-level factors. The similarity in pediatric/adult placebo trajectories is robust but does not address potential differences in active treatment effects. The clinical significance is primarily for trial methodology rather than patient care.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These findings can guide sample size calculations and endpoint selection in future ADHD trials but do not alter current clinical practice regarding placebo response management.

item.title: [9] The Impact of Psychological Therapies on Well-Being and Quality of Life in Adult Chronic Migraine Patients: A Systematic Review.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: Chronic migraine (≥15 headache days/month, ≥8 migraine days) severely impairs quality of life and is often complicated by insomnia and emotional distress. This systematic review examined whether psychological therapies (mindfulness, CBT for insomnia) improve well-being and quality of life in adults with chronic migraine.
FINDINGS: Four heterogeneous studies were included (mindfulness-based interventions and CBTi). Mindfulness reduced headache frequency and disability, improved pain acceptance and mood, and showed sustained benefits up to 12 months post-intervention; combining mindfulness with tDCS suggested additive effects. CBTi improved sleep quality and led to delayed but meaningful reductions in headache days. Emotional outcomes (depression) improved modestly; anxiety outcomes were inconsistent.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is very small (only four studies) and heterogeneous in interventions and outcomes, precluding meta-analysis. Methodological limitations include lack of blinding, small samples, and variability in comparators and follow-up durations. While results suggest psychological therapies may improve several domains of functioning, the strength of evidence is low and prone to bias. Larger, well-controlled RCTs with standardized outcomes are needed to confirm efficacy and identify which patients benefit most.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current findings do not justify changing first-line migraine treatments but suggest psychological therapies—particularly mindfulness and CBTi—could be considered as adjuncts in multidisciplinary care for motivated patients with chronic migraine and comorbid insomnia or mood symptoms.

item.title: [7] Neuroscience-informed psychoeducation for bipolar disorder.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The chapter reviews neuroscience-informed psychoeducation (NIPE) for bipolar disorder, integrating neural mechanisms (prefrontal-limbic dysfunction, reward processing, circadian disruption) into psychoeducational content. It aims to bridge neuroscience with clinical practice but lacks empirical evaluation of NIPE’s efficacy in bipolar disorder.
FINDINGS: The review outlines NIPE’s theoretical framework, translating neural mechanisms into psychoeducational strategies (e.g., cognitive monitoring, circadian interventions). It proposes mechanisms for improved outcomes (e.g., adherence, self-efficacy) but notes no randomized trials or robust empirical data exist to confirm these benefits.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence is purely theoretical, with no direct clinical data. Strengths include a plausible mechanistic rationale and practical delivery considerations (e.g., state-dependent insight). However, the lack of empirical validation, potential biases (e.g., narrative review), and untested assumptions limit confidence. The proposed effect sizes and clinical relevance remain speculative.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: NIPE may offer a promising adjunct to bipolar psychoeducation, but its use should be considered experimental. Clinicians should await randomized trials before adopting NIPE, as current recommendations are based on mechanistic plausibility rather than proven efficacy.

item.title: [6] Risk of falls and delirium associated with dual orexin receptor antagonists versus benzodiazepines and Z-drugs in older adults with dementia.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study compared safety outcomes (falls, delirium, hospitalisation, mortality, and emergency department visits) between dual orexin receptor antagonists (DORAs) and benzodiazepines (BZDs)/Z-drugs in older adults (≥65 years) with dementia and insomnia, using retrospective electronic health record data. The clinical question is whether DORAs are safer alternatives to BZDs/Z-drugs in this high-risk population.
FINDINGS: In 734 propensity score-matched pairs (mean age 83.5 years; 65–66% female), DORA use was associated with significantly lower risks over 12 months: falls (HR 0.35, 95% CI 0.18–0.71; P = 0.003), delirium (HR 0.39, 95% CI 0.23–0.65; P < 0.001), hospitalisation (HR 0.31, 95% CI 0.21–0.47; P < 0.001), and emergency department visits (HR 0.32, 95% CI 0.20–0.50; P < 0.001). Mortality showed no significant difference (HR 0.77, 95% CI 0.53–1.11; P = 0.154).
INTERPRETATION: This retrospective cohort study provides moderate-strength evidence suggesting DORAs may reduce falls, delirium, and healthcare utilisation compared with BZDs/Z-drugs in older adults with dementia. However, residual confounding is likely due to the observational design (e.g., unmeasured illness severity, prescribing bias). The large effect sizes (HRs ~0.3–0.4) are clinically meaningful but should be interpreted cautiously. Confirmation via prospective randomised trials is needed before practice changes.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: DORAs may represent a safer option than BZDs/Z-drugs for insomnia in older adults with dementia, potentially reducing falls and delirium. Clinicians should consider this evidence when weighing risks/benefits but await stronger evidence before definitive practice changes.

item.title: [6] Neuroscience-informed psychoeducation for depression: From stress to adaptive brain recovery.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This narrative review explores whether neuroscience-informed psychoeducation (NIPE)—which integrates contemporary affective neuroscience, stress biology, neuroplasticity, and brain-circuit research into patient education—can improve outcomes for adults with major depressive disorder (MDD) by enhancing understanding, self-management, and engagement with treatment.
FINDINGS: The paper synthesizes evidence on conventional psychoeducation in mood disorders and argues that NIPE may reduce self-blame and stigma, strengthen agency, and support sustained recovery by framing depression as a disorder of adaptive brain recovery. No quantitative outcomes (e.g., effect sizes, p-values) are reported, as this is a narrative review rather than a trial or meta-analysis.
INTERPRETATION: As a narrative review, the evidence is conceptual and lacks direct empirical data. Strengths include integration of recent neuroscience and clinical rationale; limitations include absence of systematic evidence synthesis, no quantitative estimates, and potential selection bias in cited studies. The clinical significance of NIPE remains unproven pending controlled trials.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: NIPE may offer a theoretically sound adjunct to standard psychoeducation, but current evidence does not justify changing practice. Clinicians may consider it as a communication tool while awaiting empirical validation.

item.title: [6] Concomitant Psychotropic Medication Is Associated with Reduced Outcomes of Trauma-Focused Psychotherapy for Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study examined whether concomitant psychotropic medication at the start of trauma-focused psychotherapy for PTSD reduces treatment efficacy in a real-world cohort. Using target-trial emulation with double machine learning and inverse probability weighting, it assessed changes in CAPS-5 scores from pre- to post-treatment in 6,125 adults receiving standardized trauma-focused therapy at a Dutch center (2021–2024).
FINDINGS: Mean CAPS-5 scores improved by 25.7 points overall (Cohen’s d = −2.30). Psychotropic co-medication (n = 1,382) was associated with a 2.52-point smaller improvement (−9.4%, 95% CI −10.0 to −8.9; d = −1.11, E = 10.0) versus no co-medication. The negative association persisted at 6-month follow-up (d = −0.42). Antidepressants (d = −0.28; follow-up d = −0.56), amitriptyline, mirtazapine, anticonvulsants, antipsychotics, fluoxetine, zolpidem, and zopiclone showed consistent associations with poorer outcomes across sensitivity analyses.
INTERPRETATION: The study used robust target-trial emulation and sensitivity analyses to mitigate confounding, suggesting a modest but consistent reduction in psychotherapy efficacy with certain psychotropic co-medications. However, the observational design precludes causal inference, and effect sizes, while statistically significant, may not translate into clinically dramatic differences. Unmeasured confounding and selection bias remain possible despite E-value robustness.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These findings suggest clinicians may consider tapering or substituting specific psychotropic medications—particularly certain antidepressants and sedatives—before initiating trauma-focused psychotherapy to optimize outcomes. Routine practice should balance this potential benefit against risks of medication discontinuation and relapse. Further randomized trials are needed to confirm causality and guide tapering strategies.

item.title: [15] Beyond scales: Artificial intelligence, language, and behavior in suicide risk modeling-a narrative review.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This narrative review examines whether artificial intelligence (AI) methods—machine learning, deep learning, and large language models—can improve the identification of individuals at imminent suicide risk by integrating diverse data sources (EHRs, clinical notes, speech, neuroimaging, passive sensing). It focuses on clinically relevant performance metrics, validation practices, and implementation challenges in routine psychiatric care.
FINDINGS: The review synthesizes evidence across multiple data modalities (structured records, natural language processing, speech/behavioral signals, neuroimaging, and passive sensing) to assess AI’s potential in predicting suicidal thoughts and behaviors. It highlights the need for robust discrimination and calibration metrics, temporal and external validation, and interpretable outputs for clinical decision-making. Key barriers include class imbalance, label noise, dataset shift, limited prospective evaluation, and ethical concerns such as privacy, bias, and governance.
INTERPRETATION: As a narrative review, this study does not provide quantitative effect sizes or head-to-head comparisons but instead maps the landscape of AI applications in suicide risk prediction. The strength of the evidence lies in its comprehensive overview of modalities and methodological challenges, while its weakness is the lack of systematic quality assessment or pooled estimates. The clinical relevance of AI tools remains uncertain until prospective, externally validated studies demonstrate improved patient outcomes.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current AI models are not yet ready for routine use in suicide risk stratification; clinicians should remain cautious about adopting unvalidated tools. Future priorities include multimodal longitudinal cohorts and pragmatic trials to assess whether AI decision support improves prevention outcomes and care pathways.

item.title: [12] Bridging Inpatient and Community Care Following First Episode Psychosis: A Pilot Feasibility and Acceptability Study of a Brief Psychological Intervention.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study assessed whether a brief CBT-informed psychological intervention could be feasibly delivered to young adults with first-episode psychosis (FEP) transitioning from inpatient to community care, and whether it was acceptable to patients. This was a single-arm pilot feasibility and acceptability study conducted in a specialist early intervention inpatient unit over seven months.
FINDINGS: Of 43 patients screened, 38 were eligible; 28 (74%) consented, 6 (15%) disengaged, and 17 (44%) completed all six sessions and outcome measures. Mean patient satisfaction was 4.76/5. Qualitative feedback emphasized continuity of care, coping skills, and making sense of the admission and recovery. The study was not powered to assess clinical effectiveness.
INTERPRETATION: The study demonstrates feasibility and high acceptability of a brief CBT-informed intervention delivered across inpatient and community settings, with reasonable recruitment and retention rates for a pilot. However, as a single-arm, uncontrolled pilot with no clinical outcome evaluation, the evidence is preliminary and subject to selection and attrition biases. The lack of a comparator and small sample limit conclusions about effectiveness or generalisability to broader FEP populations.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: This pilot supports the practicality of delivering brief CBT-informed support during the inpatient-to-community transition for FEP, but does not yet justify changing practice; further controlled trials are needed to assess clinical benefit and long-term outcomes.

item.title: [10] Obsessive-Compulsive and Related Disorders in the Middle East and North Africa Region: A Scoping Review.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: Obsessive-compulsive and related disorders (OCRDs) are under-recognised and undertreated in the Middle East and North Africa (MENA) region. This scoping review mapped published evidence on OCRDs across MENA countries to identify research patterns and gaps.
FINDINGS: 393 studies from 13 MENA countries (1991–2025) were included; 304 came from Iran. Sample sizes ranged from 6 to 29,858 (median ≈ 106.5, mean ≈ 407). OCD dominated clinical samples, followed by BDD. 142 therapeutic studies covered pharmacotherapy, psychotherapy and neuromodulation; 136 epidemiological studies focused mainly on OCD and BDD.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is growing but uneven, with heavy concentration in Iran and sparse data from many MENA countries. Most studies are observational or small trials; heterogeneity in design and quality limits synthesis. Cultural adaptation of tools and region-specific policies are needed, but current evidence is insufficient for firm clinical recommendations.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Clinicians should be aware that OCRD research in MENA is patchy and largely Iranian; extrapolating findings to other countries may be unreliable. Routine screening and culturally adapted care remain justified, but high-quality trials are urgently needed.

item.title: [7] A Mixed-Method Feasibility Study of an Online Group Program for Pregnant Women With ADHD.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This mixed-methods feasibility study assessed the acceptability and preliminary impact of AMOR, a 10-week online group psychoeducation program for pregnant women with ADHD in Denmark, using pre/post questionnaires and qualitative interviews.
FINDINGS: Fifty-seven women self-referred within 3 months; 32 were enrolled, 27 completed the program (84.4% retention), and 25 completed follow-up (92.6%). Mean session attendance was 80%. Satisfaction was high (CSQ mean 25.76; 88% would recommend). Negative effects were infrequent and mild. Quantitative changes in symptom measures were small, with modest improvements in anxiety and ADHD-related quality of life.
INTERPRETATION: The study demonstrates strong feasibility and acceptability of AMOR, supported by high recruitment, retention, satisfaction, and qualitative endorsement. However, the uncontrolled design and small, self-selected sample limit causal inference and generalisability. The observed symptom changes are modest and may reflect non-specific effects; definitive conclusions about clinical effectiveness await RCTs.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: AMOR appears promising as a well-tolerated, patient-valued perinatal support for women with ADHD, but should currently be considered experimental pending efficacy trials. Clinicians may cautiously offer it as an adjunct while monitoring for individual benefit.

item.title: [15] Interventions to reduce perinatal suicidality: a global systematic review.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This global systematic review (PROSPERO registered) asked whether non-pharmacological interventions can reduce perinatal suicidality (ideation, plans, attempts) in pregnant or postpartum women. Only six heterogeneous studies were found, limiting the strength of any conclusion.
FINDINGS: Five RCTs (three individually randomised, one cluster, one noninferiority) and one historical controlled trial were included. Two RCTs reported reductions in suicidality: one multidisciplinary community programme and one behavioural activation therapy; one showed a significant reduction at 3–4 months postpartum that was not maintained at 7–8 months. Three studies collected suicidality data only for safety monitoring and were not powered to detect a reduction.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is extremely small (six studies, mixed designs, inconsistent outcomes) and at high risk of bias. Only two studies showed any reduction in suicidality, and one of those was not sustained. The remaining three studies were underpowered safety-monitoring exercises. No robust trial specifically targets perinatal suicidality reduction, so conclusions remain tentative.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current data do not justify changing practice; clinicians should continue standard risk assessment and management while awaiting adequately powered RCTs designed to reduce perinatal suicidality.

item.title: [11] Neurobiology of Treatment-Emergent Mania Associated with Antidepressant: A Narrative Review Update.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This narrative review examines the neurobiological mechanisms behind antidepressant-associated treatment-emergent mania (TEM) in bipolar disorder (BD), particularly why some patients develop mania after antidepressant use despite clinical guidelines advising caution. It synthesizes recent findings on how different antidepressant classes (TCAs, SSRIs, atypical agents) may trigger TEM via distinct neurochemical pathways and individual susceptibility factors.
FINDINGS: TCAs carry the highest TEM risk, linked to cholinergic-adrenergic imbalance and heightened noradrenergic activity, while SSRIs are less implicated but still associated with TEM through serotonin-related mechanisms and receptor interactions. Even atypical antidepressants (non-monoaminergic) can induce manic switches, suggesting vulnerability is key. Factors like hepatic metabolism, mitochondrial dysfunction, and immunoinflammatory processes further modulate risk. The review emphasizes that TEM reflects network-level mood dysregulation rather than a universal antidepressant effect.
INTERPRETATION: As a narrative review, this study synthesizes heterogeneous evidence without systematic quality assessment or quantitative synthesis, limiting certainty. Strengths include broad coverage of neurobiological mechanisms and antidepressant classes, but weaknesses include lack of rigorous bias assessment, reliance on secondary sources, and no direct clinical applicability. The clinical significance of these mechanisms remains uncertain due to the absence of controlled trials or effect sizes. The review highlights plausible pathways but does not establish causality or quantify risk.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current practice should continue to follow guidelines cautioning against antidepressant monotherapy in BD, especially in BD-I, with close monitoring for manic symptoms. However, this review does not change practice beyond reinforcing individualized risk assessment and vigilance, as the mechanisms and risk factors remain theoretical and unquantified.

item.title: [9] Tracing Responses to a Syndemic: A Systematic Map of Substance Use, Mental and Sexual Health Interventions for Gay, Bisexual and Other Men Who Have Sex With Men in Southeast Asia.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic map (PRISMA-ScR) examined intervention studies addressing the syndemic of substance use, mental health, and sexual health among gay, bisexual, and other men who have sex with men (GBMSM) in Southeast Asia (2010–2024), aiming to identify evidence gaps and inform holistic intervention design.
FINDINGS: Of 2,016 records, 142 publications described 130 studies with 148 interventions reaching 154,502 GBMSM. Most interventions (n=143) focused on sexual health (e.g., HIV testing, PrEP, treatment), while only 3 targeted mental health and 2 substance use, primarily via psychosocial approaches. Mental health outcomes were reported in 9 interventions and substance use in 5, mostly as secondary measures. Only one intervention addressed all three syndemic domains.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is heavily skewed toward sexual health, with minimal focus on mental health and substance use despite their syndemic relevance. The review highlights a critical gap in holistic, multi-domain interventions and overreliance on psychosocial strategies. Limitations include lack of standardized outcome reporting and potential publication bias toward HIV-focused research. External validity is constrained by regional funding priorities and narrow intervention types.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current practice in Southeast Asia is dominated by HIV-centric interventions, leaving unmet needs in mental health and substance use for GBMSM. Clinicians should advocate for integrated, syndemic-responsive care models, but robust evidence for such approaches is currently lacking.

item.title: [6] [Pharmacological treatment options for adult attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder].
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This is a narrative review summarizing pharmacological treatment options for adult ADHD, including stimulants (methylphenidate, lisdexamfetamine), non-stimulants (atomoxetine), and other agents, alongside pre-treatment assessments and long-term management considerations. The clinical relevance lies in the high prevalence of underdiagnosed adult ADHD and its associations with functional impairment, psychiatric comorbidities, and long-term somatic risks.
FINDINGS: The review highlights methylphenidate and lisdexamfetamine as first-line stimulant options, with atomoxetine as a non-stimulant alternative, particularly for patients with comorbid substance use or anxiety. It emphasizes the need for baseline cardiovascular and metabolic screening before initiating pharmacotherapy and acknowledges challenges such as adherence, tolerability, and long-term safety monitoring. The authors underscore the role of multimodal treatment, including psychoeducation and psychotherapy, in optimizing outcomes.
INTERPRETATION: As a narrative review, this paper synthesizes existing evidence without systematic appraisal or quantitative synthesis, limiting the strength of its conclusions. While it provides a useful overview of treatment options and practical considerations, it does not offer effect sizes, comparative data, or rigorous risk-benefit analyses. The lack of a structured methodology (e.g., systematic search, inclusion criteria) and absence of critical appraisal of individual studies weaken its internal validity. External validity is also limited by the focus on general principles rather than specific patient populations or settings.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: This review reinforces the importance of multimodal treatment for adult ADHD but does not provide actionable comparative data to guide specific drug choices. Clinicians should use this as a general framework for treatment planning while relying on higher-quality evidence (e.g., guidelines, RCTs) for individualized decisions. Watch for emerging data on long-term outcomes and safety, particularly regarding cardiovascular and metabolic risks.
